title: Words for sex down the ages

entries.note: English's single earthy Germanic word for love, shared across sister languages, with a distant ancestor in common with Latin [[same-root:libido]] and a Sanskrit word for confusion.
Latin word meaning desire, sharing a distant ancestor with [[same-root:love]].
Sanskrit word related to [[same-root:love]] that the hosts say means confusion, which they find telling.
Entered English in the 13th or 14th century from Old French for a verse narrative or knightly hero's journey; vernacular tales of knights and their loves made it mean love story.
The French word for a novel, showing that all novels are romances in a way; see [[same-root:romance]].
German term for a coming-of-age story, another kind of [[same-root:roman]].
Used interchangeably with early Romance for the people's version of Latin rather than the classical one; see [[see:romance]].
In [[see:Vulgar Latin]] it means of the common people, not rude.

Borrowed from French; it meant the categories of the sexes and only came to mean intercourse in the 1800s. It implies division, like [[same-root:section]], [[same-root:sect]] and [[same-root:insect]].
Shares a root with [[same-root:sex]].
An Old English word for sex meaning a thing shared, a euphemism of sorts.
Related to [[same-root:sex]], which implies a division between the sexes.
Related to [[same-root:sex]], which implies a division between the sexes.
Middle English term for sex; the suffix -red was an alternative to -ship, so it amounts to [[see:fellowship]].
What [[see:fellowred]] amounts to, since -red could be used instead of -ship.
Old verb for having sex with someone, used by [[see:Geoffrey Chaucer]] in [[see:The Miller's Tale]]; Rob dislikes it.
Used [[see:swive]] in [[see:The Miller's Tale]]: 'thus swived was the carpenter's wife'.
Chaucer's tale of adultery about an old carpenter whose wife sleeps with the lodger, quoted for [[see:swive]].
Literally means to lead someone away.
Old euphemistic phrase for having sex, found in texts describing exhausted men.
Originally a dance, it was a popular term for sex in the 1600s and 1700s but was little used afterwards.
Phrase for sex, evoked by [[see:the shaking of the sheets]].

To play at hot cockles was a 17th-century phrase for having sex, quoted from 1687.
Appears in the 1687 [[see:hot cockles]] quote about a furious husband, showing that the notion of horniness is old.
Euphemism for sex used from the 1600s onwards.
Sex term in Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue, glossed as a rogering bout and named after [[from:Moll Peatly]].
A fabled sex worker, also called Moll Prattley, whose name gives [[gave:Moll Peatly's jig]]; the reference was meant to be pejorative.
An old word for sex that Rob particularly dislikes.
A 1600s term for sex.
Victorian term; to firkytoodle meant to mess about or take liberties. Jess likes it.
One of the old terms for sex in Rob's list.
One of the old terms for sex in Rob's list.
One of the old terms for sex in Rob's list.
One of the old terms for sex in Rob's list.
Rob's favourite old term for sex, as if you just slipped.
Probably the most clinical term for sex, yet still euphemistic because it means a coming together.
Called definitely euphemistic, in contrast with [[see:coitus]].
Jess's joke coinage for a more precise term naming the two body parts, modelled on [[see:cunnilingus]].
Euphemism for sex and reproduction from spring imagery, around since the 1600s and perhaps popularised by an 1825 poem by [[see:Samuel Taylor Coleridge]].
His 1825 poem about bees and birds stirring in spring may have helped popularise [[see:the birds and the bees]].
Perhaps the most literal term for a sexual act, meaning vulva licking.
The 17th-century English term for [[equivalent:cunnilingus]].
Mild in northern England but nearly as offensive as the C word in the south, as [[see:David Cameron]]'s radio gaffe showed.
The British prime minister famously said [[see:twat]] on the radio.
Older than expected, probably from an Italian word for delight or perhaps from [[from?:diddle]]; an earlier nonsense word in ballads like [[see:fa la]], also discussed before.
A less elegant theory derives [[gave?:dildo]] from a corruption of diddle.
A ballad filler implying something else happened, comparable to the earlier nonsense use of [[see:dildo]].
[[see:Thomas Nashe]]'s poem, one of the first to use [[see:dildo]], about a man who hands his dildo to a prostitute.
Wrote [[see:The Choice of Valentines]], one of the first poems featuring [[see:dildo]].
A musical filler phrase, as in 'hey nonny nonny', listed in the historical thesaurus as a word for the vulva and popular in the 1600s.
Famous translator who glossed Italian [[see:fossa]] as a woman's [[see:pleasure pit]] or [[see:nonny-nonny]].
Italian word that [[see:John Florio]] translated as a woman's [[see:pleasure pit]].
[[see:John Florio]]'s term for the vulva in his translation of [[see:fossa]].
A fairly literal word for the vulva from the 1200s.
A 1600s word for the vulva, also bugle-boo, quoted from a poem on [[see:Hero and Leander]].
A poem quoted for [[see:bugle-bow]]: 'one hand he put upon her toe, the other on her bugle-bow'.
The Victorian term for the vulva.
An occasional term for the vulva.
Old English word for the penis; the ending means 'little', and the first part might mean pin.
Term for the penis in the 1500s, often paired with [[see:coney]] for the vulva, as in a ferret hunting rabbits in a warren.
A word for a rabbit long used as a euphemism for the vulva, helped by its similarity to Latin [[see:cunnus]] and rabbits' prolific sex lives.
The Latin word for the vulva, whose resemblance to [[see:coney]] helped make that word a euphemism.
An STD named from [[from:clapper]], previously discussed, which meant both a rabbit warren and a brothel where you might catch it.
Meant both a rabbit warren and a pleasure house, giving [[gave:the clap]].
Named after rabbits, from [[from:coney]], which once meant a little rabbit.
In the 1600s it was common to call the penis and testicles your bagpipe.
An alternative old term for the male genitals, found in Rob's research.
Originally baseball slang for a gaffe, short for [[from:bonehead]], later extended to an erection.
Shortened to give the baseball sense of [[gave:boner]].
A short thick penis, also an insult, from around the 1950s; dubiously traced to a Navajo word for penis or a Hindi or Bengali word for copulate.
Supposedly from Yiddish [[from:shlang]], meaning snake.
Most likely originally meant something like tail, like a common German word for it.
With the earlier coochie, popularised by [[see:Willie Dixon]]'s 1954 song [[from:Hoochie Coochie Man]]; it goes back to the [[from:hoochie coochie]] dance.
[[see:Willie Dixon]]'s 1954 song, full of innuendo, which popularised [[gave:cooch]].
Popularised [[see:cooch]] with his 1954 song [[see:Hoochie Coochie Man]].
Belly-dance-inspired number at the 1893 World's Fair linked to [[see:Little Egypt]]; the name may come from [[from?:Hoochie Coochie Rice]] or [[from?:The Ham Fat Man]].
Performer said to have inspired the [[see:hoochie coochie]] dance, though whether she was at the 1893 fair is debated.
Minstrel show performer whose stage name may have influenced the name of the [[see:hoochie coochie]] dance.
Song containing the phrase 'hoochie coochie coochie', a possible influence on [[see:hoochie coochie]].
Example of a reduplicative term like [[see:hoochie coochie]].
Not vulgar; a backslang shortening of [[from:fanny]], spread through [[see:Polari]] and [[see:Round the Horne]]. The 'not available for fucking' backronym is false.
Gay slang, discussed before, through which [[see:naff]] entered English usage.
Radio show full of [[see:Polari]] that introduced [[see:naff]] to a British public unaware it was gay slang.
Means the front in Britain, where it is mild, but the back in America; probably a name euphemism like [[see:Johnson]].
Name euphemism for the penis, compared with [[see:fanny]].
Sister word to [[see:fanny]]: in France it means the front bits, in Quebec the back, the same transatlantic split.
First a small furry animal like a cat, probably imitative; linked to women from the 1600s, perhaps influenced by Old Norse for pocket; unrelated to [[unrelated:pusillanimous]].
From Latin meaning cowardly; a myth wrongly links it to the insulting sense of [[unrelated:pussy]].
Like [[see:catfight]], applied to women, showing the link between women and cats behind [[see:pussy]].
Like [[see:catty]], applied to women, showing the link between women and cats behind [[see:pussy]].
Almost a compliment, unlike the insult [[see:pussy]], though both say the same thing.
First a bend in rope or hair, then a mental deviation, as in [[see:Thomas Jefferson]]'s 'kink in their heads'; the sexual sense appears by the mid-1900s.
Wrote of judges taking 'a kink in their heads', using [[see:kink]] for a mental deviation.
Coined by [[see:Friedrich Salomon Krauss]] and made clinical by the APA in the 1980s; para- means alongside or against, as in [[see:paranormal]] and [[see:parachute]].
The sexologist who named some sexual kinks [[see:paraphilia]]s.
Turning a human into furniture, for example tying them up and sitting on them.
Sexual attraction to, or pleasure from, stealing.
Sexual interest in gigantism or excessive growth.
Sexual interest in small things.
Sexual attraction to cars and machines.
Sexual interest in poetry, which Rob jokingly takes to mean sex with the London Underground.
Sexual interest in obscene words.
Has the same para- as [[see:paraphilia]], meaning alongside.
Has the same para- as [[see:paraphilia]], meaning alongside.
Has the para- of [[see:paraphilia]], with a sense of alongside but also against.
From a Portuguese word for charm, sorcery or allurement; still an object thought to have supernatural power. The sexual sense came in the 1800s, largely through [[see:Havelock Ellis]].
Wrote many problematic books about sex and largely brought the sexual sense into [[see:fetish]] in the 1800s.
German Jewish gynaecologist who fled the Nazis, developed the [[see:Gräfenberg ring]] IUD, and had the [[gave:G-spot]] named after him in 1981.
Named in 1981, after his death, after [[from:Ernst Gräfenberg]], though he had nothing to do with that area of gynaecology.
[[see:Ernst Gräfenberg]]'s name for his early intrauterine device, a ring rather than today's T shape.
From Greek [[from:orgasmos]], excitement or swelling, first used of animals in heat or ripening fruit; in 17th and 18th-century English it mostly described women's orgasms.
Greek for ladder; its use as a synonym for [[see:orgasm]] is partly thanks to [[see:Marie Stopes]].
Palaeobotanist and women's rights activist who helped make [[see:climax]] mean orgasm and founded Britain's first birth control clinic.
Sanskrit for thread of love; a 2,000-year-old book by [[see:Vatsyayana]] about wealth, merit and pleasure, known in English from an 1883 translation.
The author of the [[see:Kama Sutra]], written around the first century.
One of the [[see:Kama Sutra]] sex positions in English translation.
A [[see:Kama Sutra]] position; Jess thinks it sounds like something witches do in the woods.

A concept the language allows but has no word for, like a non-virgin, the couple getting married, or a groom equivalent of [[see:bridal]].
Virginity is a social construct, and English has no single noun for someone who is not a virgin, a [[see:lexical gap]].
Originally used for dirty men, then transferred to sexually active women.
A word for someone with a lot of sexual experience, unlike the missing word for a non-[[see:virgin]].

Suggested for people getting married, but Rob says it doesn't name the couple at the wedding the way French [[see:mariés]] does.
Offered as the English for the bride and groom together, but not a single word like [[see:mariés]].
French word for the couple getting married, which English lacks, a [[see:lexical gap]].
Originally the compound bride-ale, a party, like [[see:scythe-ale]], which is why there's no 'groomal' and why bridal can relate to the groom.
A harvest party, showing how -ale formed party words like [[see:bridal]].
A Japanese coinage from English words for close, mostly non-sexual physical affection; it spread to Korean and then into English through K-pop and J-pop.
Fan fiction use for pairing characters, which Jess thinks helped spread all the new -ship relationship words.
A relationship of flirting that goes no further.
Mutual attraction that is never communicated.
A relationship in which you go to each other for problem solving.
A relationship aimed at fixing the partner.
A relationship where you give something to get something.
Someone you only get involved with on holiday.

The English equivalent of [[equivalent:Geschlechtsverkehr]].
German slang for sex; Jess likes it because it implies a full experience with foreplay.
Cute German slang term for sex.
German slang for sex, matched by English [[equivalent:pipe laying]].

Rob calls this German slang for sex the most German one by far.

From the Greek god of carnal love [[from:Eros]]; entered English in the 1600s and took off in the Freudian era.
Greek god of love, especially carnal love, who gives [[gave:erotic]].
Ancient Greek word for passionate physical love and desire, one of four categories of love.
Ancient Greek word for general affection, seen in words like [[see:philia]].
Example of words showing the Greek [[same-root:phileō]].
Ancient Greek word for contented, happy affection.
Ancient Greek word for love involving power dynamics, such as a parent's or ruler's love.
From Latin [[from:fornax]], oven or kiln; related to [[same-root:fornicate]], both ultimately from a root meaning to heat.
Not from heat but from [[from:fornix]], an arch, since sex workers gathered under arches like those of the [[see:Circus Maximus]].
Latin for an arch or vaulted walkway, shaped like an oven; it also meant a brothel and names an arch-shaped part of the brain.
Sex workers hung out under its arches, giving [[see:fornix]] the sense of brothel.
From Latin for bewitch, first used of witches' power to enthral; the positive sense came in the early 1800s. Probably related to [[same-root?:fascinum]].
The divine phallus, a winged symbol on Roman amulets invoking the protection of the god [[see:Fascinus]].
The phallic god whose protection the [[see:fascinum]] amulets invoked.
